source.title: SANE: The phases of gradient descent through Sharpness Adjusted Number of Effective parameters

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether Hessian-derived measures track validation loss, using correlation measures that differ from the magnitude-aware perturbation measure in V7.
record.gate_note: Reports correlations between SANE, effective parameter count (Neff), and maximum Hessian eigenvalue (λmax) and validation loss. Other reported results on learning-rate instability and Hessian shifts do not measure a behavior named by the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures correlations of Hessian-derived metrics with validation loss, not V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus the training–test error gap. It neither tests nor uses another listed version. A different sharpness metric and a different outcome do not constitute a T2 test of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors propose SANE as an effective-dimensionality measure that tracks validation loss and remains useful under unstable large-learning-rate training. They report weaker post-training correlations without early stopping and explicitly acknowledge that SANE does not address overfitting. More precisely than the record states, they report that the expected positive relationship between maximum Hessian eigenvalue and validation loss was not observed in their experiments.
record.recipe_differences: Measures Hessian-derived quantities and correlates them with validation loss; it does not perform magnitude-aware weight perturbation tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SANE-to-validation-loss correlation differs between early-stopped and final model comparisons. On CIFAR-10, the reported correlations also vary with Hessian approximation depth k.

fits_no_version.finding: SANE correlates positively with validation loss: 0.54 versus 0.42 for early-stopped versus final FMNIST models, and 0.92–0.94 versus 0.76–0.88 on CIFAR-10 across approximation depths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SANE tracks validation loss across the tested training configurations, with weaker correlations for final checkpoints than for early-stopped checkpoints.

fits_no_version.finding: Maximum Hessian eigenvalue has negative correlations with validation loss in both tables, ranging from -0.18 to -0.71. The authors explicitly report that the expected positive relationship was not observed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Raw maximum Hessian eigenvalue does not consistently predict worse validation loss in these full-batch learning-rate experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Neff correlations with validation loss are weakly negative on FMNIST and more strongly negative on CIFAR-10, especially for final checkpoints; the authors call the latter relationship unexpected.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The direction and strength of Neff's relationship with validation loss depend on the tested dataset and checkpoint selection.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 and Section 3.1 describe SANE retaining trajectory-level tracking under unstable learning rates while Neff and maximum Hessian eigenvalue deteriorate. SANE can also remain stable while validation loss rises through overfitting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SANE is more robust to instability spikes than the tested alternatives, but does not reliably detect overfitting.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code is shared in the supplementary material)
record.problems: The authors say interpretation of absolute SANE and Neff values requires more work. Correlations do not establish causality; final-model correlations degrade without early stopping. CIFAR-10 correlations use a k-layer approximation to the Hessian, and k=1 is described as highly uninformative in the supplementary discussion. Error bars are described for Figure 1, but the correlation tables provide no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical correlation result in Table 1 or Table 2 was left out. Figure-only trajectory and metric values were not transcribed as additional rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level generalization under random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.

Comparative held-out error of convolutional and fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity. Appendix C.1 compares metric trajectories across architectures without establishing this accuracy comparison.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under specified tuning budgets and recovery recipes.

Held-out performance across training batch sizes at fixed epoch budgets and with adapted recipes. Batch sizes here define reduced full-batch datasets; the study does not report the required comparison.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across data sizes, dropout strengths, or augmentation conditions.

Magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance versus training–test error gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks, including ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Synthetic eigenvector perturbations visualize output changes rather than test this relationship.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples compared with removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All tabulated values match the supplied text. The 225 FMNIST models are five seeds at 45 learning rates, with divergent trajectories excluded from correlations; the 32 CIFAR-10 models are two seeds at 16 learning rates. FMNIST uses four classes and 1,000 training examples; CIFAR-10 uses 5,000 training examples. Row states concern applicability to the listed versions, not whether the reported correlations exist. Figure-only findings were already declared omitted, and no missing result testing a listed version was identified.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and generalization on natural labels.
Widening beyond the interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and their held-out performance.
Large versus small batch training and the effects of adapting the training recipe.
Magnitude-aware weight perturbations, comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures, CIFAR-10 and SVHN without augmentation, and the stated correlation with the training–test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
